<h2>What is a method?</h2>
<p>A <strong>method</strong> is a named block of code that only runs when it is called (see the <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se17/html/jls-8.html#jls-8.4" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Java Language Specification §8.4</a> for full method declaration syntax). Procedural abstraction lets a programmer use a method by knowing what it does — from the signature and documentation — without needing to know how it was implemented internally.</p>

<h2>Method signatures</h2>
<p>A <strong>method signature</strong> identifies a method uniquely within a class. It consists of the method name plus the ordered list of parameter types. Return type is NOT part of the signature.</p>
<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Anatomy of a Method Header</h4>
  <pre>public static double average(int a, int b)</pre>
  <p><code>public static</code> — access and type modifiers<br>
  <code>double</code> — return type (what the method gives back)<br>
  <code>average</code> — method name<br>
  <code>(int a, int b)</code> — parameter list (names + types of inputs)<br>
  <strong>Signature:</strong> <code>average(int, int)</code> — name + ordered parameter types only</p>
</div>

<h3>Parameters vs Arguments</h3>
<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>The Distinction</h4>
  <p>A <strong>parameter</strong> is a variable declared in the method header. It exists inside the method body.<br>
  An <strong>argument</strong> is the actual value passed when the m
ethod is called. Arguments must match parameters in number, order, and compatible type.</p>
  <pre>// Declaration: a and b are parameters
public static double average(int a, int b) { ... }

// Call: 10 and 6 are arguments
double result = average(10, 6);</pre>
</div>

<h3>Call-by-value</h3>
<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Call-by-Value Rule</h4>
  <p>When arguments are passed to a method, the parameters are initialized with <em>copies</em> of the argument values. Changing a parameter inside the method does NOT change the original variable in the calling code.</p>
</div>
<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>Example</h4>
  <pre>public static void doubleIt(int n) {
    n = n * 2;   // changes the local copy only
}
int x = 5;
doubleIt(x);
System.out.println(x);  // still prints 5</pre>
</div>
<div class="apcsa-callout trap">
  <h4>AP Trap: call-by-value for primitives</h4>
  <p>This is one of the most-tested traps in Unit 1. Students assume the original variable changes. It does not — <code>x</code> is still 5 after the call. The primitive value was copied; the method only modified its own local copy.</p>
</div>

<h2>void vs non-void methods</h2>
<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>The Distinction</h4>
  <p>A <strong>void</strong> method performs an action but returns no value. It is called as a standalone statement: <code>System.out.println("hi");</code><br><br>
  A <strong>non-void</strong> method returns a value of the declared return type. The return value must be stored in a variable or used in an expression: <code>double avg = average(10, 6);</code></p>
</div>
<div class="apcsa-callout trap">
  <h4>AP Trap</h4>
  <p>Calling a non-void method and discarding the return value (e.g., <code>average(10, 6);</code> without storing it) compiles in Java but is almost always a logic error on the exam. Calling a void method as part of an expression is a compile error.</p>
</div>

<h2>Execution flow: method calls interrupt sequencing</h2>
<p>When a method is called, execution jumps into the method body. The calling code pauses. Once the method finishes (reaches <code>return</code> or the closing brace), control returns to the line immediately after the call.</p>

<h2>Overloaded methods</h2>
<p>Methods are <strong>overloaded</strong> when a class has multiple methods with the same name but different signatures. <code>Math.abs(int x)</code> and <code>Math.abs(double x)</code> are overloaded. Java picks the correct version based on the argument type at the call site.</p>

<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> 60</div>

<strong>A.</strong> Call-by-value means <code>n</code> is initialized with a copy of <code>score</code> (50). <code>n += 10</code> changes the local copy to 60, but <code>score</code> in the calling code is never touched. Prints 50.</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>
    </div>

  <h2>Call-by-reference for objects</h2>
  <p>Call-by-value applies to primitive types. When an object is passed to a method, the parameter receives a copy of the <em>reference</em> (memory address), not a copy of the object itself. This means the method can change the object’s internal state by calling methods on it — but it cannot make the caller’s variable point to a different object. This distinction matters in Unit 3 when you write your own classes.</p>
